content: so how do i improve creative thinking?

Here are practical, book-grounded steps to improve creative thinking, building on your earlier question about a “creative spot”:

1) Know the building blocks: treat creative thinking as moments of insight and as a process that moves through Four Stages of Creativity. Create room for each stage instead of forcing linear progress [668a799d7f7a-00064].

2) Find your Creative Sweet Spot and protect it daily: pick one cleared block of time (the author suggests experimenting with the First Hour Rule — many people are most divergent/insightful early) and use it for Generate work (divergent thinking) rather than execution [668a799d7f7a-00490][668a799d7f7a-00064].

3) Match mental state to task: learn the mental states (the book describes Seven Mental States) and deliberately choose the right state for what you’re doing — Generate for ideation, Converge/Execute later for finishing ideas [668a799d7f7a-00065].

4) Work with Creative Cycles: track your natural ups and downs and schedule demanding creative work during high-energy phases; respect low-energy phases for different types of tasks or rest so insight can incubate [668a799d7f7a-00266].

5) Use the right tools: use “grippy” tools (which resist distraction) when you need deep ideation and “slippy” tools for execution; when executing, make the slippy tool grippy only for that task if needed [668a799d7f7a-00265].

6) Prefer event-time over strict clock-time: don’t try to force outcomes into rigid time slices — use time blocks as guides to allocate creative energy toward goals, not to squeeze insight on demand [668a799d7f7a-00490].

7) Build rituals and small habits (your “personal placebo”): consistent cues and routines help you enter creative states more reliably and conserve mental energy for ideas [668a799d7f7a-00266].

A simple daily routine to try:
- Block your Creative Sweet Spot (start with 30–60 minutes). Experiment with the First Hour Rule. Use a grippy tool and focus on Generate tasks.
- After ideation, step away (incubation) or switch to low-effort tasks. Later, schedule a convergent session with slippy tools to refine and execute.
- Track when you feel most creative across a week and align future blocks with that rhythm.

If you want, I can help you identify your Creative Sweet Spot (based on your daily schedule and energy patterns) and design a 2-week experiment to lock in a routine.

In this book, I share a cohesive and flexible system for managing creative
energy. This is my proposal to humanity to let go of the notion that we can
squeeze more from our time. Instead, let’s think about how to get more
from our minds.
We’ll start, in the next chapter, with the single building block of creative
thinking – the moment of insight. If we understand what a creative insight
is, and how insightful thinking differs from analytical thinking, we can
know how to create the conditions for insight to happen. We’ll find your
Creative Sweet Spot, so you can do your best creative thinking when the
time is right.
Then, we’ll break down the creative process. Creative work is so
unpredictable because progress doesn’t happen linearly. Instead, our
creative projects iterate through the Four Stages of Creativity. If we learn
what these stages are, and how to create room for them, we can stop
struggling to achieve solutions, and start letting those solutions come to us.

lookout for time worship. Time usually isn’t what you’re optimizing for.
Work according to clock-time only when it really matters. Otherwise, work
according to event-time. Don’t try to cram certain outcomes into units of
time. Instead, use units of time as rough guides to allocate your energy into
activities that will move you toward your goals.

content: i am addicted to my phone how do i prevent these distractions and focus

Practical, book-grounded steps to beat phone addiction and protect focus — with a short 2-week experiment you can try.

Steps to start today
1) Schedule offline (deep) blocks and explicit Internet blocks. Decide when you’ll next allow yourself to use the phone, then don’t use it until that time — this strengthens your attention muscles and prevents constant switching [8a642cf3d808-00311][8a642cf3d808-00317].

2) Put the phone physically away during offline blocks. Keep it out of reach or in another room, or use airplane/Do Not Disturb so it cannot intrude (physical distance reduces the reflex to check) [8a642cf3d808-00317][8a642cf3d808-00304].

3) Embrace boredom. When you resist the urge to check, you rebuild tolerance for low-stimulation moments and reduce on-demand distraction habits that make deep focus impossible [8a642cf3d808-00311][8a642cf3d808-00304].

4) Quit or severely limit social media and other network tools that fragment attention. Either remove apps, log out, or schedule long, infrequent social-media blocks rather than leaving them always available [8a642cf3d808-00349].

5) Use the right tools for the mental state you want. For idea generation or deep thinking, choose “grippy” tools that resist distraction (pen & paper, single-purpose apps). If you must use a “slippy” tool (phone/computer), deliberately make it grippy for the session (app blockers, focus modes, single-app fullscreen) [668a799d7f7a-00242][668a799d7f7a-00265].

6) Build a simple ritual to cue focus (e.g., clear desk, put phone in drawer, 2-minute breathing, start timer). Rituals conserve willpower and make entering a focused state easier over time [668a799d7f7a-00265].

7) Track and iterate. Note when you felt tempted, how long you lasted, and which tactics helped. Align deep blocks with your high-energy creative times (your Creative Sweet Spot) [668a799d7f7a-00265].

A 2-week experiment (easy, repeatable)
- Week 1: Start with one daily deep block of 30 minutes (preferably early). Before you begin, set the next Internet block time (e.g., 45–60 minutes after starting). Put your phone in another room or on airplane mode. Use a grippy tool (not the phone) for ideation [8a642cf3d808-00311][668a799d7f7a-00242].
- Week 2: Increase to two deep blocks (30–60 min each). Add a rule: no social apps outside scheduled Internet blocks; use an app blocker or remove apps if needed. Track cravings and note improvements in focus [8a642cf3d808-00349][668a799d7f7a-00265].

If you want, I can:
- design a personalized 2-week schedule based on your daily routine and energy peaks, or
- suggest specific phone settings/apps (Focus modes, app lockers) and a short ritual to start each deep block.

The idea motivating this strategy is that the use of a distracting service does not, by
itself, reduce your brain’s ability to focus. It’s instead the constant switching from
low-stimuli/high-value activities to high-stimuli/low-value activities, at the slightest
hint of boredom or cognitive challenge, that teaches your mind to never tolerate an
absence of novelty. This constant switching can be understood analogously as
weakening the mental muscles responsible for organizing the many sources vying for
your attention. By segregating Internet use (and therefore segregating distractions)
you’re minimizing the number of times you give in to distraction, and by doing so you
let these attention-selecting muscles strengthen.

sensitive communication into your offline blocks (e.g., texting with a friend to agree on
where you’ll meet for dinner), as well as time-sensitive information retrieval (e.g.,
looking up the location of the restaurant on your phone). Outside of these pragmatic
exceptions, however, when in an offline block, put your phone away, ignore texts, and
refrain from Internet usage. As in the workplace variation of this strategy, if the
Internet plays a large and important role in your evening entertainment, that’s fine:
Schedule lots of long Internet blocks. The key here isn’t to avoid or even to reduce the
total amount of time you spend engaging in distracting behavior, but is instead to give
yourself plenty of opportunities throughout your evening to resist switching to these
distractions at the slightest hint of boredom.
